extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetics/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and aesthetic principles for assessing and producing poetry (distinguishing simple vs sentimental poetry, satire, elegy, tragedy vs comedy, didactic limits, and the role of nature and the ideal). Useful for critics, teachers, and practicing poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic faculty rooted in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is the only flame that kindles and warms the poetic soul; the poetical faculty obtains all its force from nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should be ultimately rooted in the 'necessity of nature' and the moral instinct that returns man to nature. Even when cultured or artificial, poetic activity must speak to or derive strength from nature; otherwise it risks losing the poetic spirit. Examples/implication: authentic poetic feeling arises from sensuous unity and an original harmony of feeling and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two legitimate modes of poetic genius: imitation of the real vs representation of the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: In a state of natural simplicity the poet's part is 'to imitate the real as completely as is possible.' In the civilized state the poet's task is 'to raise reality to the ideal' or 'to represent the ideal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both modes are valid manifestations of poetic genius; evaluate poets by which mode they pursue and how well they realize it. This distinction underpins the difference between ancient (finite/real) and modern (infinite/ideal) poetic temperaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate wit or cleverness with poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: It is incorrect to apply the expression poetic to any of the so‑styled productions of wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating cleverness, variety of forms, or mere display of talent as equivalent to poetic depth. True poetry requires a union of sensuous feeling and thought (or an engagement with the ideal), not just stylistic brio or witty effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate by spirit not accidental form
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare poets 'not according to the accidental forms which they may have employed, but according to their spirit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging ancient vs modern (or different schools), prioritize the poet's underlying spirit and aim (addressing nature vs addressing the civilized/ideal) rather than surface genre, meter, or topical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match medium to what it can render: sensuous limits vs imaginative infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: An object addressing the eyes is perfect in proportion as it is clearly limited; a work addressed to the imagination can reach perfection by means of the ideal and the infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that plastic/visual arts benefit from determinate, finite representation, while poetic (imaginative) arts can exploit the infinite/ideal. Thus expect different comparative strengths across media (ancients superior in plastic arts; moderns stronger in ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple poetry: unity of origin and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: In simple poetry the feeling we experience is 'absolutely identical' across lyric, epic, dramatic or descriptive forms; differences are only in degree, not quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When poetry springs directly from sensuous intuition and imitates reality, judge it by the sincerity and intensity of the single feeling it evokes rather than by formal variety. The unity of effect is a hallmark of 'simple' poetic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimental (reflective) poetry involves dual principles—real and ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentimental poet 'reflects on the impression produced on him by objects' and is concerned with two opposite forces: the real (limited) and the ideal (infinite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentimental poet must decide which principle predominates (satirical/aversion to the real, or elegiac/attachment to the ideal). Evaluate consistency in handling this duality; the resulting mixed feeling should be deliberate and coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: subject is distance from nature and contrast between reality and ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is a satirist when he takes as subject 'the distance at which things are from nature, and the contrast between reality and the ideal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire must awaken the ideal in the reader; mere material grumbling or personal bitterness is an anti‑pattern. Two modes: avenging/pathatic satire (serious, moral indignation) and sportive/humorous satire (playful wit). Each must maintain poetic substance: pathetic satire should assume the sublime; playful satire must envelope its theme in beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic pathos must derive from the ideal, not from material interest
rubrics_metrics.description: All pathos derived from purely sensuous or material interest is 'unworthy of poetry'; poetry ought only to move us 'through the medium of ideas' and reach the heart via reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting personal grievances, sensual obstacles, or mere frustration masquerade as poetic indignation. True poetic emotion raises the reader toward moral independence and freedom of mind (example: Tacitus' elevated judgement of Roman decadence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone alignment: seriousness vs playfulness must be subordinated to poetic form
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of poetry is not compatible either with the tone of punishment or that of amusement; pathetic tone is too grave for play, amusement too trifling for seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve the tension by making pathetic satire sublime in character, and ensuring playful satire acquires poetic substance and beauty. The poet's tone should preserve poetic form (freedom of movement and elevation toward the ideal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal interest; maintain impersonal poetic feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: All personal interest, and reference to a personal necessity, should be banished from poetic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic expression should be oriented toward universal/ideational concerns rather than private complaint or vindication. Even when lamenting real losses, the poet must transfigure them into ideal losses to retain poetic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: To depict revolting or low reality, ground it in necessity and elevate viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: When representing 'some revolting reality' the essential thing is that 'the necessary be the foundation' and that the poet 'disposes our mind for ideas' from an elevated point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an elevated moral/intellectual vantage so the depiction awakens the ideal in readers (example: Tacitus). Simply wallowing in low facts without the idealizing disposition is anti‑poetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs tragic method: comic poet sustains aesthetic character himself; tragic poet is aided by theme
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedy the theme in itself does much; in comedy the object does nothing and the poet all. Tragedy treats its theme practically and seeks heart interest; comedy treats it theoretically and appeals to the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comedians on their sustained elevated tone and capacity to preserve freedom of mind without lapsing into pathos; assess tragic poets by their ability to suspend freedom and then re‑establish it aesthetically. Classification depends on the tribunal before which the work is judged (not merely on subject matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of comedy: preserve and cultivate freedom of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The noble task of comedy is to produce and keep up in us this freedom of mind; comedy aims at liberating man from violent passions and enabling a calm, lucid survey of himself and the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should avoid inducing suspension of freedom (pathos) and instead use wit and understanding to correct vice or absurdity. Evaluate how well a comic work cultivates equanimity and rational perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of genuine poetic worth: endurance under difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an infallible test to discriminate natural facility of manner from ideal gentleness: trials presented by difficulty and events offering great opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius that is merely facile will collapse into platitude under pressure; true poetic worth reveals itself in demanding circumstances and by sustained inner seriousness. Use challenging material or form to reveal the poet's depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious moral purpose underlie the best satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious intention may be detected under malicious jests; satire that 'avenges truth against sophistry' and combats for an ideal is elevated (examples: Lucian, Aristophanes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate satire not only for its comic surface but for whether a higher moral/ideal aim animates it. Without such seriousness, raillery may amuse but not move as poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegiac poetry: sadness (elegy) or joy (idyl) must arise from enthusiasm for the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the poet opposes nature to art and the ideal to the real, and the pleasure taken in them is dominant, he is elegiac. Either nature and ideal are objects of sadness (elegy) or both are objects of joy (idyl).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegy should spring from an idealized sense of loss rather than from mere sensual deprivation; external complaints (e.g., exile laments) are insufficient unless transfigured into an idealized mourning (anti‑pattern: Ovid's exile poems are criticized for lacking 'spirit and nobleness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegiac complaint must make the finite an ideal loss
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of poetic complaint 'ought never to be an external object, but only an internal and ideal object; even when it deplores a real loss, it must begin by making it an ideal loss.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic lamentation should universalize and spiritualize particular losses—transform memory and historical particulars into emblems of transitoriness and the infinite. Assess elegies by their capacity to transfigure particulars into ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of thought and feeling; avoid being the spectator of one's own emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet must combine the activity of thought and feeling so that the 'proper activity of thought should show itself mixed more with feeling, and the sensuous more with thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a poet is primarily a spectator of his own emotion (reflecting thought about feeling rather than communicating feeling), the emotional impact is weakened (example: Haller's elegy where the poet 'becomes thus a spectator of his own emotion'). Strive for immediacy and integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of didactic poetry: thought must be raised to the ideal to be poetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Didactic poetry can only be conceived when super‑sensuous themes pass from the finite to the infinite and become objects of spiritual intuition; otherwise 'the thought itself of these poems is not poetical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Didactic subjects risk losing poetry unless the intellectual content is poetically transfigured—imagination must serve understanding without reducing poetry to pure doctrine. A didactic poem in which thought itself remains poetic is rare; evaluate such works for their imaginative transformation of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance teaching and painting: prefer poetic depiction over didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets like Haller 'constantly teach rather than paint'; even when painting, 'his brush is more energetic than lovable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or writing, prefer imagery and sensuous depiction that embody ideas over overt instruction. Excessive didacticism steals away sensuous charm and beauty—assess works for whether they 'paint' (evoke) rather than merely 'teach.'
